newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan hopes IMF will resume lending programmes.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan hopes IMF will resume lending programmes.

text.p: A Pakistani official said on Thursday he hoped to convince the International Monetary Fund to resume stalled lending programmes during talks in Washington later this month.
"We are taking a package of measures for the discussions and hope we will be able to reach an agreement," said V.A. Jafarey, finance adviser to Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto.
"They (the IMF) will review our estimates of the budgetary situation," he told a news conference.
Jafarey said the discussions planned for September 28 would focus on reviving a stalled $600 million standby loan and an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF).
The IMF withheld payment of an $80 million tranche of the standby loan, due to have been disbursed in June, pending a review of Pakistan's budget for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).
Jafarey said Pakistan had completed its own review of the budget figures, but declined to give details of any revisions.
He said Pakistan still wanted to cut the fiscal deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from more than five percent in 1995/96, despite some adjustments in revenue collection plans.
Jafarey described Pakistan's foreign exchange position as satisfactory, with cash reserves of $1.4 billion and gold deposits worth about $800 million.

He said the trade deficit in the first two months of 1996/97 had narrowed to a provisional $500 million from $630 million in the year-ago period. Exports had risen 14.9 percent, but imports only by 1.6 percent, he added.
Pakistan's trade gap grew to about $3 billion last year from $2.25 billion in 1994/95.
The IMF halted a three-year, $1.5 billion ESAF programme in 1995 after Bhutto's government failed to meet agreed targets for deficit reduction and tariff reform.
